key_insight: A digital-twin-inspired time-to-event model combines longitudinal ALS functional scores with survival analysis to predict individualized disease progression and wheelchair-free survival.
clinical_relevance: The model could help clinicians anticipate when assistive devices may be needed, supporting earlier care planning, trial stratification, and personalized follow-up.
method: Harmonized longitudinal ALS data: diagnosis, ALSFRS-R, activities of daily living, and demographics.
Clustered function into domains and modeled nonlinear decline with generalized additive mixed models.
Built a temporal machine learning + Cox time-to-event framework to generate individualized survival curves and predict wheelchair access.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports a harmonized longitudinal cohort and multiple modeling approaches, with lower limb function—especially walking and stair climbing—emerging as the strongest predictors of earlier wheelchair use.
watch_item: Performance, external validation, and real-world generalizability are not described in the abstract, so deployment would need careful prospective testing.
paper_title: A Temporal Machine Learning-Based Time-to-Event Model for Predicting ALS Progression and Healthcare Utilization
